sections.rawHeading: 1 · Licensing (GOV — high confidence; a real registration regime)
sections.title: State licensing and registration
sections.confidenceNote: high confidence; a real registration regime
sections.markdown:
**Rhode Island is the outlier of northern New England: it actually requires contractors to register with the state, and chimney work is covered.** The **Contractors' Registration and Licensing Board (CRLB)**, in the Dept. of Business Regulation, administers **R.I. Gen. Laws chapter 5-65**, which requires **every contractor, remodeler, and most subcontractors who build or repair residential/commercial structures and their appurtenances to register before working on a structure (§ 5-65-3)** — and the enumerated subcontractors who must register **explicitly include "Masons, including chimney installers, fireplace installers, and general masonry erectors"**, so chimney work is named in the statute itself. "A city, town, or the state shall not issue a building permit to anyone required to be registered under this chapter who does not have a current, valid registration or valid license" (§ 5-65-3). Registrants must carry **public liability and property damage insurance of $500,000 combined single limit** plus workers' comp as required (§ 5-65-7). **Neither § 5-65-3 nor § 5-65-7 imposes a bond** — do not publish a bond amount. The CRLB line: it **registers** general contractors (no competency exam) and **licenses** only commercial roofers, home inspectors, underground utility, water filtration, well drilling and pump installers — **there is no CRLB chimney license**, so chimney contractors register. Public lookup: **crb.ri.gov/consumer/search-registrantlicensee**.
**A second, chimney-adjacent credential (DLT, not CRLB):** the Dept. of Labor and Training's pipefitter/sheet-metal rules (**260-RICR-30-15-2, § 2.22(I)**, authority R.I. Gen. Laws § 28-27-7) create a **Decorative Heating Appliances Limited II** license covering "gas fired logs; gas, pellet, or wood decorative appliances and their related flue connections and terminations; replacement flue liners for residential installations only." Applicants **"must hold a current certification from the National Chimney Sweep Guild or the National Fireplace Institute"** plus a notarized statement of two years' experience; fuel piping is not allowed under it, and municipal permits are issued to the licensee. That makes RI one of the rare states where a state license **requires a chimney-industry certification** — but only for that limited appliance/liner scope. *(Whether this license is mandatory for every liner or stove install, versus one route among pipefitter/sheet-metal licenses, is not confirmed — say "a state license for this work exists and requires NCSG or NFI certification," not "required for all liner jobs.")* This is the strongest chimney-relevant credential structure in the batch.

sections.title: What the credential does not test
sections.markdown: Narrower than the no-license states but still real. CRLB **registration** verifies identity, insurance, and a registry entry — **not flue diagnosis or masonry competence** (registration, unlike specialty licensure, requires no exam). A registered contractor may never have inspected a chimney. Individual certs (CSIA CCS, C-DET; NCSG CCP/CCR) remain the competence signal, but here "check the registration at crb.ri.gov" is a genuinely useful first step — more than it is in NH/VT/ME.

sections.rawHeading: 3 · Home sale (GOV — high confidence; explicit chimney + fireplace line items)
sections.title: Seller disclosure when a home sells
sections.confidenceNote: high confidence; explicit chimney + fireplace line items
sections.markdown: Rhode Island has a **genuinely strong, chimney-naming mandatory disclosure.** **R.I. Gen. Laws § 5-20.8-2** requires the seller of a 1–4 unit residence to deliver a written disclosure **"as soon as practicable, but in any event no later than prior to signing any agreement to transfer"** — and the statute's item list **separately itemizes "Fireplaces — (Number, Working and Maintenance, Defects)" (§ 5-20.8-2(b)(3)(vi)), "Chimney — (Maintenance History, Defects)" ((b)(3)(vii)), and "Heating System — (Type, Imp. & Repairs, Underground Tanks, Zones, Supplemental Heating, Defects, Modifications)" ((b)(3)(xiv)).** Actual-knowledge standard; each violation carries a **civil penalty up to $1,000 per occurrence (§ 5-20.8-5)**. That is a real, chimney-specific disclosure. No general inspection is mandated at transfer (but see §6's CO certificate); NFPA 211 Level 2 stays a NATIONAL STANDARD.

sections.title: Consumer remedies and cancellation rights
sections.markdown: The **Deceptive Trade Practices Act (Unfair Trade Practice and Consumer Protection Act), R.I. Gen. Laws chapter 6-13.1**, gives AG enforcement and a private right of action for damages. Door-to-door sales are separately governed by the **Door-to-Door Sales Act, chapter 6-28**, which gives a **3-day right to cancel — written notice by midnight of the third day after signing, excluding Sundays/holidays (§ 6-28-3)** — and **failure to return a deposit exposes the seller to DOUBLE damages (§ 6-28-4)**. That is the exact mechanic against chimney scare-sales. Complaints: RI AG Consumer Protection Unit.

sections.title: Permits and building codes
sections.markdown: Rhode Island has a **statewide State Building Code**; the one- and two-family code **RISBC-2 (510-RICR-00-00-2) adopts the 2021 IRC** with RI amendments (current version listed effective Dec 1, 2025 on the Secretary of State's rules site). Because registration is tied to permits (§ 5-65-3 bars permits to unregistered contractors), chimney relines, rebuilds, crowns, and solid-fuel appliance installs that require a permit also require a registered contractor. Routine sweeps and like-for-like caps generally are not permit work. RI is small and comparatively uniform, so less local patchwork than the other three states.

sections.rawHeading: 6 · CO law (GOV/DOC — high on requirement; UNVERIFIED on exact section)
sections.title: Carbon monoxide and smoke alarm law
sections.confidenceNote: high on requirement; UNVERIFIED on exact section
sections.markdown: Unusually strong at transfer — **but the citation is unverified.** Under the **RI Fire Safety Code (R.I. Gen. Laws ch. 23-28.1 et seq. and the state fire code regulations; note ch. 23-28 itself is repealed)**, all occupied residential properties must have smoke and CO detectors (installed per NFPA 72 / NFPA 720), and — the standout — **at transfer of title the seller must give the buyer a certificate from the local fire department stating the smoke/CO systems were inspected within 60 days prior and found in good working order**, with a ~$30 inspection fee borne by the seller. CO alarms are required where there are fuel-burning appliances, fireplaces, or an attached garage. This is a genuine **pre-sale fire-department CO/smoke inspection certificate** — the strongest transfer-time CO regime in the batch and a direct tie-in to a chimney/stove check. *(The precise section for the pre-sale certificate, the 60-day window and the ~$30 fee are all UNVERIFIED — chapter 23-28 is repealed and the requirement likely lives in chapter 23-28.1 or the adopted fire code regulations; confirm before publish.)*

sections.title: Solid fuel and environmental rules
sections.markdown: Rhode Island has meaningful but lower wood-heat share than NH/VT/ME. No statewide burn-ban or stove-emission regime beyond federal EPA new-stove standards (NATIONAL STANDARD). Not a material statutory section for RI; 1–2 sentences and move on.

sections.rawHeading: 8 · Scam landscape (REF — partial; pull specifics before publish)
sections.title: Scam patterns and enforcement
sections.markdown: The RI AG's Consumer Protection Unit pursues home-improvement fraud, and the door-knock "we were in the neighborhood / noticed your chimney" pitch is a textbook chapter 6-28 + 6-13.1 violation; here it is **also** an unregistered-contractor problem, since unregistered work is barred under § 5-65-3. Regional New England reporting has tied chimney-sweep scams to weak trade regulation elsewhere — but RI's CRLB is the counterexample. **Specific RI chimney-sweep enforcement actions: NOT YET CONFIRMED — re-run search before publish.**

story.heading: The story
story.markdown: Rhode Island **BREAKS the master correlation — and breaks it in the "strong-on-both" direction that's rarer than the weak-on-both cases.** The rule predicts a state either licenses hard and discloses little, or licenses nothing and discloses a lot. Rhode Island does **both**: it requires contractors (masons included) to register with the CRLB and bars permits to the unregistered, AND its seller-disclosure form names the chimney and the fireplace as separate line items, AND (reportedly — section still being verified) it demands a fire-department smoke/CO inspection certificate at the closing table. For a state this small, that is an unusually complete consumer stack. The catch the page should flag: CRLB **registration** carries no competency exam, so "registered" still is not "qualified" — which is exactly the gap individual certs and an independent audit fill.

faq.q: What should I check before hiring a chimney company in Rhode Island?
faq.a: State licensing: YES-ish — CRLB REGISTRATION required (R.I. Gen. Laws § 5-65-3; "masons, including chimney installers, fireplace installers"; no exam; no CRLB chimney license) + DLT Decorative Heating Appliances Limited II license requiring NCSG/NFI cert (260-RICR-30-15-2.22(I)). Registration or credential: YES — CRLB registry, permits barred to unregistered contractors. Seller disclosure at sale: YES — § 5-20.8-2, form names Fireplaces + Chimney + Heating separately (penalty $1,000/occurrence). Right to cancel a sale made at your home: YES (Door-to-Door Sales Act § 6-28-3; double damages § 6-28-4). Carbon monoxide alarm law: STRONG (reported) — pre-sale fire-dept smoke/CO certificate (exact section, 60-day window UNVERIFIED). Where to check a contractor: crb.ri.gov + riag.ri.gov complaints. Then ask the eight questions below, get the inspection findings in writing with photos, and never sign for "emergency" work on the day of a door-knock.
